passages.title: Listen before joining others
passages.summary: Solomon’s opening teaches a learner to hear parents. Wisdom warns people against joining violent men.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me explains fearing God as love and obedience. Why does Wisdom warn that the violent men trap themselves?

contextNote.title: Wisdom begins with relationships
contextNote.text: The opening places instruction in the voices of a father and mother. Their teaching competes with the invitation of a violent group. The reader must choose whose words to trust. Wisdom concerns the company one keeps as well as individual choices. Learning begins before the short sayings start.

passages.title: Search for wisdom
passages.summary: The teacher urges the learner to seek understanding. Wisdom guards against dishonest men and unfaithful partners.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me invites readers to seek wisdom from God. Which actions does the teacher compare with searching for treasure?

contextNote.title: Learning requires a search
contextNote.text: Hidden treasure gives instruction the shape of a demanding search. The resulting wisdom protects paths and relationships rather than merely adding information. This chapter joins effort in learning with judgment about where to walk.

passages.title: Trust God and help neighbors
passages.summary: The teacher urges trust in God, generous giving, and kind treatment of neighbors.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me teaches trust in the Lord. Why should the learner help a neighbor today rather than tomorrow?

contextNote.title: Trust reaches a neighbor’s need
contextNote.text: The chapter moves from trust in God to duties toward nearby people. Delaying available help exposes the practical stakes of that trust. Wisdom must govern an ordinary decision about another person’s immediate need.

passages.title: Choose a path carefully
passages.summary: A father recalls his own father’s teaching. He warns against joining people who harm others.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects the path image with following the Lord. How do speech, sight, and steps affect the path the learner follows?

contextNote.title: A father repeats what he received
contextNote.text: The speaker recalls being taught before instructing the next generation. That memory gives teaching a history within the household. Images of paths then make inherited instruction something the learner must actively follow.

passages.title: Remain faithful to your wife
passages.summary: The teacher warns against adultery, sex that breaks marriage promises. He urges delight in one’s wife.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: What costs does the teacher describe beyond the first attraction?

contextNote.title: Water images distinguish shared commitment from wandering
contextNote.text: The chapter compares marital faithfulness with drinking from one’s own supply. Its positive image follows warnings about ruinous desire. Read the passage’s pleasure and boundaries together rather than treating it only as prohibition.

passages.title: Promises, work, and harmful acts
passages.summary: The teacher warns about unpaid debts, laziness, lying, and adultery. He describes ants preparing food.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: How does the ant’s work differ from the sleeper’s choices?

contextNote.title: Different dangers share a need for attention
contextNote.text: The ant example stands beside debt warnings and descriptions of harmful conduct. Each section exposes damage before its full cost arrives. The chapter asks readers to notice habits and commitments that can quietly constrain them.

passages.title: A learner follows a tempting invitation
passages.summary: The teacher watches a young man meet a married woman. She persuades him to follow her.
passages.uncertainty: Egypt names the cloth’s origin, not the scene’s location.

lds.text: Which details show the difference between her promises and the danger?

contextNote.title: A warning unfolds as a scene
contextNote.text: The speaker watches a young man rather than merely naming a forbidden act. Timing, speech, and movement show persuasion gathering force. The ending makes the observer’s account a warning to the present listener.

passages.title: Wisdom speaks in public
passages.summary: Wisdom calls people to listen. She describes fair rule and her presence before God formed the earth.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me points to the rejection of evil in verse 13. How does Wisdom’s public invitation differ from the woman’s invitation in chapter 7?

contextNote.title: Wisdom speaks beyond the household
contextNote.text: Wisdom addresses public places and describes her relation to creation. Her voice connects ordinary judgment with the order of the world. The poem expands instruction beyond one parent’s advice to one child.

passages.title: Two women invite the learner
passages.summary: Wisdom prepares a meal and invites learners. Folly offers stolen food while hiding death.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: What does Folly hide that Wisdom openly explains?

contextNote.title: Similar invitations conceal different endings
contextNote.text: Wisdom and Folly both invite those who lack understanding. Their parallel calls make first impressions inadequate for choosing. The meals must be judged by where each host leads the guest.

passages.title: Words and work affect others
passages.summary: Sayings compare honest work with laziness, truthful words with lies, and care with hatred.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: How does hatred stir up quarrels while love covers offenses?

contextNote.title: Short sayings require a supplied situation
contextNote.text: The book now places brief contrasts beside one another. A saying about many words invites readers to imagine an actual conversation. Its force depends on applying the contrast rather than expecting a continuous plot.

passages.title: Honesty in trade and community
passages.summary: Sayings condemn false weights, gossip, and withholding grain. They praise fair trade and generous help.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: How does withholding grain affect the people who need it?

contextNote.title: A proverb makes trade a moral decision
contextNote.text: A false balance can hide harm within ordinary buying and selling. This saying places that practice under God’s judgment. Its short form expects the reader to supply a real situation. Read it beside the chapter’s claims about honesty and wealth. Wise conduct includes the measures that other people must trust.

passages.title: Correction, work, and careful speech
passages.summary: Sayings praise learning from correction, caring for animals, and speaking words that heal.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Why does the chapter compare rash speech with a sword?

contextNote.title: Words can wound or heal
contextNote.text: A comparison between reckless speech and a weapon gives language bodily consequences. Healing speech answers that harm rather than simply sounding pleasant. The surrounding sayings connect careful judgment with how people treat each other.

passages.title: Choose teachers and companions
passages.summary: Sayings discuss patient work, delayed hope, good companions, and parents correcting children.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Scripture Helps applies the rod image to loving, consistent teaching. How does verse 23 challenge blaming every poor person for poverty?

contextNote.title: Delay gives desire a bodily cost
contextNote.text: The saying about deferred hope names a pain that advice can overlook. Fulfilled desire then becomes a tree associated with life. This pair recognizes waiting as an experience, not only a test of discipline.

passages.title: Look beyond first impressions
passages.summary: Sayings compare careful thought with quick anger. They describe hidden grief and mistreatment of poor people.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Why should the learner look beyond laughter when judging someone’s happiness?

contextNote.title: Appearance can conceal grief
contextNote.text: Laughter does not guarantee the absence of sorrow. That observation complicates judgments made from visible behavior alone. Read it beside sayings that warn about paths which seem right at first.

passages.title: Answer gently and accept advice
passages.summary: Sayings praise gentle answers, careful listening, and loving homes. They warn against anger and greed.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me teaches kind words and patient answers. How do gentle words change the direction of a quarrel?

contextNote.title: Speech changes the direction of conflict
contextNote.text: A gentle answer and harsh words produce opposite movements in anger. The contrast concerns a response within an encounter. Later sayings about listening and counsel broaden that attention to how judgment develops.

passages.title: Plans need humility and self-control
passages.summary: Sayings discuss God weighing motives, rulers judging fairly, and pride preceding a fall.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me applies these sayings to how people communicate. Why does the chapter value controlling anger above capturing a city?

contextNote.title: Planning does not give complete control
contextNote.text: The chapter repeatedly sets human plans beside divine direction. Its statements recognize intention without making outcomes entirely available to the planner. That tension remains relevant when the sayings turn to royal judgment.

passages.title: Peace, friendship, and fair judgment
passages.summary: Sayings praise quiet homes and lasting friends. They warn against gossip, bribery, and unfair judgments.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: How do repeated accusations damage a friendship?

contextNote.title: Peace changes the value of abundance
contextNote.text: A dry piece of food can be preferable to a troubled feast. The contrast measures a household through its relationships rather than its supplies. Later sayings about friendship and quarrels develop that different scale of value.

passages.title: Listen before answering
passages.summary: Sayings warn against answering too soon. They describe arguments, unreliable wealth, and a faithful friend.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Why should a judge hear more than the first person’s account?

contextNote.title: A hearing must precede judgment
contextNote.text: Answering before listening makes speech a source of shame. Another saying notes that a first account can seem persuasive. Together they require readers to distinguish hearing a claim from testing it.

passages.title: Wealth changes how people treat neighbors
passages.summary: Sayings describe friends abandoning poor people. They praise patience, generosity, and teaching children.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: How does the chapter expose friendships that depend on wealth?

contextNote.title: Wealth can distort friendship
contextNote.text: The contrast between rich and poor people exposes unequal social attention. Companionship may follow resources rather than faithful care. This observation makes the chapter’s calls for generosity more than advice about money.

passages.title: Trade honestly and avoid revenge
passages.summary: Sayings warn about wine, false weights, careless promises, and paying back harm.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: What does the buyer’s changed story reveal about his honesty?

contextNote.title: Fair judgment begins in ordinary tools
contextNote.text: Different weights and measures allow unequal treatment to hide inside trade. The saying makes those small tools answerable to divine judgment. Nearby warnings about deceit connect outward transactions with concealed intention.

passages.title: Justice matters more than offerings
passages.summary: Sayings discuss fair conduct, dishonest wealth, ignored cries, and plans for battle.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Why does the chapter place fair conduct above an offering?

contextNote.title: Ritual cannot substitute for justice
contextNote.text: The chapter places righteous judgment above sacrifice. That comparison tests visible devotion against treatment of other people. Repeated warnings about pride and injustice prevent wealth from becoming the only measure of success.

passages.title: A good name and fair treatment
passages.summary: Sayings compare a good name with riches. A new teaching section warns against robbing poor people.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Scripture Helps teaches loving correction and rejects using the rod to justify abuse. Why does the teacher mention God when forbidding harm to poor people?

contextNote.title: A shared maker limits social divisions
contextNote.text: Rich and poor people meet within a common relation to God. The chapter still recognizes differences in influence and opportunity. Its warnings about exploiting the poor address real power rather than equal access to resources.

passages.title: Control appetite and protect others’ property
passages.summary: The teacher warns about deceptive hosts, chasing wealth, taking land, and repeated drunkenness.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Why does the teacher warn against entering the fields of fatherless children?

contextNote.title: Hospitality may carry a hidden price
contextNote.text: The guest is warned to notice a host’s divided intention. Food and flattering speech can conceal calculation. Several table scenes make appetite a question of judgment about relationships and power.

passages.title: Rescue people and examine your work
passages.summary: The teacher urges rescue of people facing death. He warns against delighting in an enemy’s fall.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: What excuse does the teacher reject when someone needs rescue?

contextNote.title: Knowing creates a duty to act
contextNote.text: The instruction about endangered people rejects a claim of ignorance. Responsibility includes what a person notices and chooses to do. The chapter places this concern beside warnings against admiring those who cause harm.

passages.title: Hezekiah’s men collect Solomon’s sayings
passages.summary: Hezekiah’s men copy sayings about rulers, disputes, friendship, and helping enemies.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: What does feeding a hungry enemy require beyond winning an argument?

contextNote.title: Collected sayings connect wisdom with government
contextNote.text: The heading names the copying of earlier sayings under Hezekiah. The chapter then addresses rulers, disputes, and restrained conduct. Its arrangement presents learning as work that can serve public judgment.

passages.title: Choose when to answer foolish speech
passages.summary: Sayings warn both against answering a fool and against leaving foolish claims unanswered.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: How can the two warnings in verses 4–5 fit different situations?

contextNote.title: Paired sayings require judgment
contextNote.text: Verse 4 warns against answering a fool in the same manner. Verse 5 then warns against leaving foolish claims unchallenged. Their placement requires judgment about the situation. Proverbs cannot always be applied as one rule with no context. Wisdom includes deciding which danger needs an answer now.

passages.title: Care for friends and flocks
passages.summary: Sayings praise honest friends and nearby help. They urge careful attention to sheep and goats.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Why does the teacher connect daily care for animals with the household’s future?

contextNote.title: Care requires knowledge of actual conditions
contextNote.text: The instruction to inspect flocks follows warnings about uncertain wealth and status. Livelihood depends on attention to living resources. This ending connects foresight with repeated care rather than a single profitable decision.

passages.title: Honest poverty and harmful wealth
passages.summary: Sayings compare honest poor people with crooked rich people. They condemn rulers who exploit the weak.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Which actions show that a wealthy person has harmed poorer neighbors?

contextNote.title: Profit can reveal a damaged relationship
contextNote.text: The saying about gain through interest questions where accumulated wealth should finally go. Other verses connect poverty with rulers and unfair treatment. The collection therefore examines the means of gaining wealth as well as its amount.

passages.title: Rulers, anger, and teaching children
passages.summary: Sayings connect fair rulers with public joy. They warn against bribery, uncontrolled anger, and neglected children.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: How does hearing a poor person’s case affect a ruler’s work?

contextNote.title: Justice requires learning the poor person’s case
contextNote.text: The righteous person knows the cause of those with little power. Indifference is presented as a failure of understanding. Nearby sayings about rule make that knowledge part of public responsibility.

passages.title: Agur asks for enough
passages.summary: Agur admits limited understanding. He asks for enough food and describes lessons from animals.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Why does Agur ask for neither poverty nor riches?

contextNote.title: A prayer questions both extremes of wealth
contextNote.text: Agur asks for neither poverty nor riches. Each condition brings a different danger to his relation with God. The prayer treats enough as a serious goal rather than a lesser form of success.

passages.title: A mother advises a king
passages.summary: Lemuel recalls his mother’s warning about drink and unfair judgment. A poem praises a capable woman.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me praises the woman’s strength, skill, and influence. How do the woman’s business decisions help both her household and poor neighbors?

contextNote.title: A mother’s instruction reaches public judgment
contextNote.text: The king is told to speak for people unable to defend themselves. The later household poem also praises work beyond private comfort. Both sections connect honor with material care and recognized contributions.

events.detail: The contrast between rich and poor people exposes unequal social attention. Companionship may follow resources rather than faithful care. This observation makes the chapter’s calls for generosity more than advice about money.

lds.text: How does the chapter expose friendships that depend on wealth?

events.title: Trade honestly and avoid revenge
events.summary: Sayings warn about wine, false weights, careless promises, and paying back harm.
events.detail: Different weights and measures allow unequal treatment to hide inside trade. The saying makes those small tools answerable to divine judgment. Nearby warnings about deceit connect outward transactions with concealed intention.

lds.text: What does the buyer’s changed story reveal about his honesty?

events.title: Justice matters more than offerings
events.summary: Sayings discuss fair conduct, dishonest wealth, ignored cries, and plans for battle.
events.detail: The chapter places righteous judgment above sacrifice. That comparison tests visible devotion against treatment of other people. Repeated warnings about pride and injustice prevent wealth from becoming the only measure of success.

lds.text: Why does the chapter place fair conduct above an offering?

events.title: A good name and fair treatment
events.summary: Sayings compare a good name with riches. A new teaching section warns against robbing poor people.
events.detail: Rich and poor people meet within a common relation to God. The chapter still recognizes differences in influence and opportunity. Its warnings about exploiting the poor address real power rather than equal access to resources.

lds.text: Scripture Helps teaches loving correction and rejects using the rod to justify abuse. Why does the teacher mention God when forbidding harm to poor people?

events.title: Control appetite and protect others’ property
events.summary: The teacher warns about deceptive hosts, chasing wealth, taking land, and repeated drunkenness.
events.detail: The guest is warned to notice a host’s divided intention. Food and flattering speech can conceal calculation. Several table scenes make appetite a question of judgment about relationships and power.

lds.text: Why does the teacher warn against entering the fields of fatherless children?

events.title: Rescue people and examine your work
events.summary: The teacher urges rescue of people facing death. He warns against delighting in an enemy’s fall.
events.detail: The instruction about endangered people rejects a claim of ignorance. Responsibility includes what a person notices and chooses to do. The chapter places this concern beside warnings against admiring those who cause harm.

lds.text: What excuse does the teacher reject when someone needs rescue?

events.title: Hezekiah’s men collect Solomon’s sayings
events.summary: Hezekiah’s men copy sayings about rulers, disputes, friendship, and helping enemies.
events.detail: The heading names the copying of earlier sayings under Hezekiah. The chapter then addresses rulers, disputes, and restrained conduct. Its arrangement presents learning as work that can serve public judgment.
events.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: What does feeding a hungry enemy require beyond winning an argument?

events.title: Choose when to answer foolish speech
events.summary: Sayings warn both against answering a fool and against leaving foolish claims unanswered.
events.detail: Verse 4 warns against answering a fool in the same manner. Verse 5 then warns against leaving foolish claims unchallenged. Their placement requires judgment about the situation. Proverbs cannot always be applied as one rule with no context. Wisdom includes deciding which danger needs an answer now.

events.title: Care for friends and flocks
events.summary: Sayings praise honest friends and nearby help. They urge careful attention to sheep and goats.
events.detail: The instruction to inspect flocks follows warnings about uncertain wealth and status. Livelihood depends on attention to living resources. This ending connects foresight with repeated care rather than a single profitable decision.

lds.text: Why does the teacher connect daily care for animals with the household’s future?

events.title: Honest poverty and harmful wealth
events.summary: Sayings compare honest poor people with crooked rich people. They condemn rulers who exploit the weak.
events.detail: The saying about gain through interest questions where accumulated wealth should finally go. Other verses connect poverty with rulers and unfair treatment. The collection therefore examines the means of gaining wealth as well as its amount.

lds.text: Which actions show that a wealthy person has harmed poorer neighbors?

events.title: Rulers, anger, and teaching children
events.summary: Sayings connect fair rulers with public joy. They warn against bribery, uncontrolled anger, and neglected children.
events.detail: The righteous person knows the cause of those with little power. Indifference is presented as a failure of understanding. Nearby sayings about rule make that knowledge part of public responsibility.

events.title: Agur asks for enough
events.summary: Agur admits limited understanding. He asks for enough food and describes lessons from animals.
events.detail: Agur asks for neither poverty nor riches. Each condition brings a different danger to his relation with God. The prayer treats enough as a serious goal rather than a lesser form of success.

events.title: A mother advises a king
events.summary: Lemuel recalls his mother’s warning about drink and unfair judgment. A poem praises a capable woman.
events.detail: The king is told to speak for people unable to defend themselves. The later household poem also praises work beyond private comfort. Both sections connect honor with material care and recognized contributions.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me praises the woman’s strength, skill, and influence. How do the woman’s business decisions help both her household and poor neighbors?

guides.title: Proverbs: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Wisdom begins with relationships
steps.text: The opening places instruction in the voices of a father and mother. Their teaching competes with the invitation of a violent group. The reader must choose whose words to trust. Wisdom concerns the company one keeps as well as individual choices. Learning begins before the short sayings start.

steps.title: A proverb makes trade a moral decision
steps.text: A false balance can hide harm within ordinary buying and selling. This saying places that practice under God’s judgment. Its short form expects the reader to supply a real situation. Read it beside the chapter’s claims about honesty and wealth. Wise conduct includes the measures that other people must trust.

steps.title: Paired sayings require judgment
steps.text: Verse 4 warns against answering a fool in the same manner. Verse 5 then warns against leaving foolish claims unchallenged. Their placement requires judgment about the situation. Proverbs cannot always be applied as one rule with no context. Wisdom includes deciding which danger needs an answer now.
